Scientific Method and Characteristics of: Hypothesis
A testable, falsifiable proposed explanation for an observation
Independent variable
The factor a researcher deliberately changes in an experiment
Dependent variable
The factor that is measured and may respond to the change
Control group
The group that does not receive the treatment, used for comparison
Homeostasis
Maintaining a stable internal environment despite external change
Metabolism
The sum of all chemical reactions occurring in an organism
Theory
A well-tested explanation supported by a large body of evidence
Quantitative data
Numerical measurements such as mass, length, or count
Qualitative data
Descriptive observations that are not numerical
Stimulus
Any change in the environment that produces a response in an organism
Biochemistry and Macromolecules: Carbohydrate
Macromolecule of sugars used for quick energy and structure
Lipid
Nonpolar macromolecule used for long-term energy storage and membranes
Protein
Macromolecule of amino acids that performs most cellular work
Nucleic acid
Macromolecule such as DNA or RNA that stores genetic information
Monomer
A single small subunit that links to form a polymer
Dehydration synthesis
Joining monomers by removing a water molecule
Hydrolysis
Breaking a polymer apart by adding a water molecule
Enzyme
A protein catalyst that lowers the activation energy of a reaction
Substrate
The specific molecule an enzyme acts upon
Active site
The region of an enzyme where the substrate binds
Denaturation
Loss of a protein's shape and function due to heat or pH change
Amino acid
The monomer subunit of proteins, containing an amine and carboxyl group
Cell Structure and Function: Nucleus
Organelle that stores DNA and directs cell activities
Mitochondria
Organelle that produces ATP through cellular respiration
Ribosome
Structure that assembles amino acids into proteins
Endoplasmic reticulum
Network of membranes that transports and modifies proteins and lipids
Golgi apparatus
Organelle that packages and ships proteins from the cell
Lysosome
Organelle containing digestive enzymes that break down waste
Chloroplast
Plant organelle that converts light energy into glucose
Cell wall
Rigid outer layer of cellulose found in plant cells but not animal cells
Cytoplasm
The gel-like fluid filling the cell where organelles are suspended
Vacuole
Storage organelle, very large and central in plant cells
Prokaryote
A cell without a membrane-bound nucleus, such as a bacterium
Eukaryote
A cell with a membrane-bound nucleus and organelles
Cell Transport and Homeostasis: Diffusion
Movement of particles from high to low concentration without energy
Osmosis
Diffusion of water across a semipermeable membrane
Passive transport
Movement across a membrane that requires no cellular energy
Active transport
Movement against the concentration gradient using ATP
Hypertonic solution
Solution with higher solute concentration than the cell, causing water loss
Hypotonic solution
Solution with lower solute concentration than the cell, causing water gain
Isotonic solution
Solution with equal solute concentration, so no net water movement
Endocytosis
Process where a cell engulfs material by folding its membrane inward
Exocytosis
Process where vesicles fuse with the membrane to expel material
Selective permeability
Property allowing a membrane to let some substances pass but not others
Phospholipid bilayer
Two-layer membrane structure with hydrophilic heads and hydrophobic tails
Photosynthesis and Cellular Respiration: Process converting light energy, carbon dioxide, and water into glucose
Process breaking down glucose with oxygen to release ATP
Adenosine triphosphate, the immediate energy currency of the cell
Green pigment that absorbs light energy for photosynthesis
Photosynthesis stage in the thylakoid that produces ATP and NADPH
Photosynthesis stage in the stroma that fixes carbon into sugar
First stage of respiration, splitting glucose into two pyruvate in the cytoplasm
Respiration stage in the mitochondrial matrix that releases carbon dioxide
Membrane process using electron flow to generate most ATP
Occurring without oxygen, such as fermentation
Anaerobic pathway that regenerates NAD+ producing lactic acid or ethanol
Cell Division: Mitosis and Meiosis: Mitosis
Nuclear division producing two genetically identical diploid cells
Meiosis
Division producing four genetically varied haploid gametes
Chromosome
A condensed structure of DNA and protein carrying genetic information
Chromatid
One of two identical halves of a duplicated chromosome
Centromere
The region where sister chromatids are joined
Interphase
The longest phase, where the cell grows and copies its DNA
Prophase
Phase where chromosomes condense and the nuclear envelope breaks down
Metaphase
Phase where chromosomes align at the cell equator
Anaphase
Phase where sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles
Telophase
Phase where nuclear envelopes reform around the separated chromosomes
Cytokinesis
Division of the cytoplasm producing two separate cells
Crossing over
Exchange of genetic material between homologous chromosomes in meiosis
Diploid
Having two complete sets of chromosomes, written 2n
Haploid
Having one set of chromosomes, written n, as in gametes
Mendelian Genetics: Gene
A segment of DNA that codes for a trait
Allele
One of several alternative forms of a gene
Genotype
The genetic makeup of an organism, such as Aa
Phenotype
The observable physical expression of a genotype
Homozygous
Having two identical alleles for a trait, such as AA or aa
Heterozygous
Having two different alleles for a trait, such as Aa
Dominant allele
An allele that masks the presence of a recessive allele
Recessive allele
An allele expressed only when no dominant allele is present
Punnett square
A grid used to predict the probability of offspring genotypes
Law of segregation
Allele pairs separate during gamete formation
Law of independent assortment
Genes for different traits are inherited independently
Incomplete dominance
Heterozygote shows a blended intermediate phenotype
Codominance
Both alleles are fully and simultaneously expressed
Test cross
Breeding an unknown genotype with a homozygous recessive to reveal it
DNA, RNA, and Protein Synthesis: DNA
Double-stranded nucleic acid storing hereditary information
RNA
Single-stranded nucleic acid that carries and interprets genetic messages
Nucleotide
DNA or RNA monomer made of a sugar, phosphate, and nitrogen base
Double helix
The twisted-ladder shape of DNA described by Watson and Crick
Base pairing rule
Adenine pairs with thymine (or uracil in RNA); cytosine pairs with guanine
Replication
Copying DNA so each new cell receives a complete set
Transcription
Building an RNA copy of a DNA gene in the nucleus
Translation
Building a protein from mRNA at the ribosome
Codon
A three-nucleotide mRNA sequence specifying one amino acid
Anticodon
The tRNA triplet that pairs with a complementary mRNA codon
Messenger RNA
RNA that carries the genetic message from DNA to the ribosome
Transfer RNA
RNA that delivers specific amino acids to the ribosome
Mutation
A change in the DNA sequence that may alter a protein
Frameshift mutation
Insertion or deletion that shifts the entire reading frame
Biotechnology: DNA combined from two different sources
A small circular DNA molecule in bacteria used as a gene vector
Protein that cuts DNA at a specific recognition sequence
Technique separating DNA fragments by size using an electric field
Polymerase chain reaction, which rapidly amplifies a DNA sequence
An organism containing a gene from a different species
Producing a genetically identical copy of a cell or organism
A precise gene-editing system adapted from bacterial immunity
Identifying individuals by their unique DNA fragment patterns
Evolution and Natural Selection: Change in the heritable traits of a population over generations
Process where organisms better suited to the environment reproduce more
An inherited trait that increases survival and reproduction
An organism's relative ability to survive and produce offspring
The formation of a new and distinct species
Random change in allele frequency, strongest in small populations
Movement of alleles between populations through migration
Similar structures inherited from a shared ancestor
A reduced structure with little or no current function
Unrelated species evolving similar traits in similar environments
Related species becoming increasingly different over time
Classification and Taxonomy: Taxonomy
The science of naming and classifying organisms
Binomial nomenclature
Two-part naming system using genus and species
Species
A group of organisms that can interbreed and produce fertile offspring
Genus
A taxonomic rank grouping closely related species
Domain
The broadest taxonomic rank: Bacteria, Archaea, or Eukarya
Kingdom
Taxonomic rank below domain, such as Animalia or Plantae
Phylogenetic tree
A branching diagram showing evolutionary relationships
Dichotomous key
An identification tool using paired either-or choices
Prokaryotic domain
Bacteria and Archaea, which lack a nucleus
Cladogram
A diagram grouping organisms by shared derived characteristics
Ecology and Ecosystems: Ecosystem
All living organisms in an area plus their nonliving environment
Population
All members of one species living in the same area
Community
All the different populations living and interacting in an area
Habitat
The physical place where an organism lives
Niche
The role and resource use of a species within its ecosystem
Producer
An organism that makes its own food, usually through photosynthesis
Consumer
An organism that obtains energy by eating other organisms
Decomposer
An organism that breaks down dead matter and recycles nutrients
Food web
An interconnected network of feeding relationships
Trophic level
A feeding position in a food chain
Carrying capacity
The maximum population size an environment can sustain
Symbiosis
A close, long-term biological interaction between two species
Mutualism
A symbiotic relationship where both species benefit
Commensalism
A relationship where one benefits and the other is unaffected
Parasitism
A relationship where one benefits at the other's expense
Succession
Gradual, predictable change in an ecological community over time
Human Body Systems: Circulatory system
System transporting blood, oxygen, and nutrients through the body
Respiratory system
System exchanging oxygen and carbon dioxide with the environment
Digestive system
System breaking food into nutrients the body can absorb
Nervous system
System of neurons transmitting electrical signals to coordinate the body
Endocrine system
System of glands releasing hormones into the bloodstream
Skeletal system
System of bones providing support, protection, and blood cell production
Muscular system
System of muscles producing movement and generating heat
Excretory system
System removing metabolic waste and regulating water balance
Immune system
System defending the body against pathogens
Neuron
A nerve cell that transmits electrical impulses
Hormone
A chemical messenger transported in the blood to target tissues
Alveoli
Tiny air sacs in the lungs where gas exchange occurs
